Name: Keynesian Economics
Description: Economic theory holding that aggregate demand is the primary driver of economic output, and that governments should use fiscal and monetary policy to manage demand and prevent recessions.
Sources: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (John Maynard Keynes)
CorePrinciples: Aggregate demand determines output and employment in the short run
Markets can fail and get stuck in recessions; government must intervene
Fiscal policy: government spending and taxation to manage economic cycle
Monetary policy: interest rates to influence borrowing and investment
Animal spirits: investor psychology drives booms and busts
Paradox of thrift: individual saving can harm the collective economy
In the long run we are all dead: urgent action matters

Name: Neoclassical / Neoliberal Economics
Description: Mainstream economic paradigm emphasizing markets, price mechanisms, rational actors, and the efficiency of free markets, with neoliberalism applying this to policy through privatization and deregulation.
Sources: The Wealth of Nations (Adam Smith — classical precursor)
CorePrinciples: Rational actors maximize utility; markets aggregate preferences efficiently
Price mechanism allocates resources better than central planning
Supply and demand as fundamental economic forces
Free trade increases prosperity for all parties
Marginal analysis: decisions made at the margin
Privatization and deregulation improve efficiency
Inflation control as primary monetary policy goal
Trickle-down: growth benefits everyone through markets
Regions: Global — dominant in international institutions (IMF, World Bank)

Name: Austrian School of Economics
Description: Economic tradition emphasizing methodological individualism, subjective value theory, capital theory, and the impossibility of socialist economic calculation.
CorePrinciples: Methodological individualism: all economic phenomena explained by individual action
Subjective value theory: value is determined by individual preferences, not labor
Economic calculation problem: socialism cannot rationally allocate resources
Business cycle theory: central bank credit expansion causes booms and busts
Time preference: people prefer present goods to future goods
Spontaneous order: markets emerge from human action, not design
Praxeology: deductive method from axiom of human action

Name: Marxist Political Economy
Description: Economic analysis examining capitalism as a system of class exploitation, focusing on the labor theory of value, surplus value extraction, and the tendency of capitalism toward crisis.
Sources: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (Lenin)
CorePrinciples: Labor theory of value: labor-time is the source of all value
Surplus value: workers create more value than they receive in wages
Capital accumulation drives capitalism; profit is unpaid labor
Tendency of the rate of profit to fall
Commodity fetishism: social relations appear as relations between things
Economic crises are inherent in capitalism, not external shocks
Class struggle between bourgeoisie (owners) and proletariat (workers)
Imperialism as capitalism's geographic expansion

Name: Modern Monetary Theory (MMT)
Description: Heterodox economic theory arguing that monetarily sovereign governments that issue their own currency can never 'run out of money,' and unemployment is always a policy choice.
Sources: Monetary Theory and Policy Practice (Randall Wray)
CorePrinciples: Monetary sovereign governments (e.g., US, Japan) are currency issuers, not users
Government deficits are non-government surpluses
Inflation, not insolvency, is the real constraint on government spending
Job Guarantee: government as employer of last resort eliminates involuntary unemployment
Taxes function to create demand for currency and control inflation, not fund spending
Balance of payments: imports are a benefit, exports are a cost
Interest rate management by central bank is a policy choice, not a necessity

Name: Institutional Economics
Description: Economic approach emphasizing the role of institutions, social norms, power, and history in shaping economic behavior and outcomes, rejecting the abstraction of pure market models.
Sources: The Theory of the Leisure Class (Thorstein Veblen)
The Theory of Economic Development (Joseph Schumpeter)
CorePrinciples: Institutions (rules, norms, laws) shape economic behavior as much as prices
Path dependence: history matters; past choices constrain future options
Transaction costs are central to understanding economic organization
Property rights and legal frameworks determine economic outcomes
Commons can be managed sustainably without privatization or state control
Veblen: conspicuous consumption, not utility, drives much behavior
Evolutionary economics: economies evolve like biological systems

Name: Behavioral Economics
Description: Economic approach integrating psychological insights into economic models, demonstrating that humans systematically deviate from rational choice in predictable ways.
CorePrinciples: Bounded rationality: humans make good-enough, not optimal, decisions
Cognitive biases: systematic errors in thinking (anchoring, availability, framing)
Prospect theory: losses loom larger than gains
Status quo bias and default effects shape behavior
Nudge: choice architecture can improve decisions without coercion
Hyperbolic discounting: we overvalue the present vs. the future
Social norms and identity shape economic decisions

Name: Degrowth Economics
Description: Economic paradigm challenging growth as the primary goal of economies, arguing that sustainable wellbeing requires deliberately reducing production and consumption in wealthy nations.
Sources: Degrowth: A Vocabulary for a New Era (D'Alisa et al.)
The Entropy Law and the Economic Process (Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen)
CorePrinciples: GDP growth on a finite planet is unsustainable and harmful
Wellbeing, not growth, should be the goal of economic policy
Reduced working time and more leisure vs. more consumption
Redistribution within economies, not growth, addresses poverty
Circular economy: waste as resource, minimize throughput
Care economy: valuing unpaid work, relationships, community
Conviviality: good life defined by relationships, not things

Name: Mercantilism
Description: Early modern economic doctrine holding that national wealth consists in accumulating precious metals through a favorable balance of trade, achieved by promoting exports and restricting imports.
Sources: The Wealth of Nations critique (Adam Smith)
CorePrinciples: Nation's wealth measured by stock of gold and silver
Favorable balance of trade: exports exceed imports
State intervention in economy to maximize trade surplus
Colonies exist to supply raw materials and buy manufactured goods
Economic competition between nations is zero-sum
Strong state and navy protect trade routes and markets
Protectionism: tariffs and subsidies defend domestic industries

Name: Market Socialism
Description: Economic system combining social or worker ownership of the means of production with market mechanisms for allocation, aiming to achieve socialist goals without central planning.
Sources: On the Economic Theory of Socialism (Oskar Lange)
CorePrinciples: Worker cooperatives or social ownership replaces private firms
Market prices coordinate production and distribution
Profits distributed to workers, not private shareholders
Investment funded by public banks or social investment funds
Competition between worker-owned firms in markets
No private appropriation of surplus value
Freedom and efficiency of markets without capitalist exploitation
